This is a very concerning situation, and your instincts are right to be worried. Regardless of your brother's age or his feelings, a 17-year-old is legally a minor in most jurisdictions, and a 32-year-old adult engaging in a sexual relationship with a minor is statutory rape—regardless of consent. Your brother may feel proud or grown-up, but that doesn't change the legal reality or the inherent power imbalance. Your priority should be your brother's safety and well-being. I strongly encourage you to speak to a trusted adult, such as a school counselor, a different family member, or a child protective services hotline, who can provide guidance on how to handle this responsibly. Remaining silent could allow the abuse to continue and potentially cause lasting harm. You are not ruining anyone's life by reporting; you are protecting a minor from exploitation.

I'm a 14-year-old boy. My dad has been hitting me with a belt since I was 8. Usually it's just a few lashes on my backside when I mess up, but last week he hit me on my legs too and I got some really bad welts. He says it's discipline and that he's teaching me respect. My mom knows but she says it's normal and I just need to behave better. I don't want to get my dad in trouble or get taken away from my family. I just want it to stop. I told my friend at school and he said I should tell a teacher. Should I? I'm scared of what will happen.

I hear how scared and conflicted you are, and it's completely understandable. No one wants to see their family broken apart. But what you're describing—being hit hard enough to leave welts on your legs—is not normal discipline. It's physical abuse, and it's not your fault. Your friend gave you good advice. Telling a teacher is brave, and teachers are required to report concerns so you can get help. You don't have to decide alone: you can also call or text the Childhelp National Child Abuse Hotline at 1-800-422-4453. They are trained to listen and help you figure out next steps without forcing you into anything. You deserve to be safe, and there are people who can help stop the hitting without automatically tearing your family apart. You are not betraying your dad by asking for help—you are taking care of yourself, and that is the right thing to do.

My 16-year-old daughter has been spending a lot of time in an online chat room with a group of people who call themselves 'free thinkers.' She's become obsessed with a 24-year-old man in the group who she calls her 'mentor.' He's been sending her money, buying her gifts, and telling her that her parents are 'brainwashed sheep.' Last week she told me she's planning to run away to live with him in another state. She said she's 'in love' and I'm just trying to control her. I'm terrified. I talked to her school counselor and they said I should take away her phone and computer and monitor her more closely. But my daughter says if I do that, she'll just find another way to leave. I'm thinking about calling the police or the FBI, but I'm afraid of making her hate me forever. What should I do?

This is a very serious situation, and I strongly recommend you contact your local police or FBI field office immediately to report suspected grooming and enticement of a minor across state lines. This man's behavior—sending money, gifts, and isolating her from you—fits the pattern of an adult targeting a minor for exploitation. Your daughter's safety is the top priority; your relationship can be repaired later. Law enforcement has trained experts who can intervene without you having to play the 'bad guy.' The school counselor's advice to restrict her devices and monitor her is also sound, but do this in coordination with authorities. Calling law enforcement is not an overreaction—it's responsible parenting in this critical moment.

I need advice. My 15-year-old daughter has lost about 15 pounds in the past two months. She barely eats anything at meals, says she's just not hungry, and I've caught her exercising in her room late at night. She used to love baking with me but now she gets angry if I mention food. When I brought up taking her to the doctor, she screamed that I'm trying to make her fat and that she'll run away if I force her. Her grades are still good and she still sees friends, so maybe it's just a phase? I don't want to lose her trust. Should I back off and let her come to me when she's ready?

I can hear how much you love your daughter and how torn you feel between wanting to protect her health and her trust. The warning signs you're describing—rapid weight loss, restricted eating, secret exercise, and intense fear of gaining weight—are serious and consistent with an eating disorder like anorexia nervosa. While it's true that some teens go through phases, the combination of behaviors here is concerning, especially the physical weight loss and her reaction to the idea of medical help. Her grades and social life may still be intact, but eating disorders can be hidden and progress quickly. In my view, backing off entirely could allow the condition to worsen, which is dangerous. I think the most loving and responsible step is to take her to a doctor or a specialist in adolescent eating disorders—not to punish her, but to get her the help she needs. You can approach it with compassion: 'I'm worried about you because I love you, and I want to make sure you're healthy. Let's figure this out together.' Maintaining trust is important, but so is her safety. You don't have to force a full therapy session right away, but a medical evaluation is a non-negotiable starting point. Many parents find that involving a professional actually helps preserve the relationship, because it takes the pressure off you to be the 'bad guy' and gives your daughter a neutral support system.

My 78-year-old mother has dementia and lives with me. She wandered outside in her nightgown at 3am last week, and a neighbor found her three blocks away confused and crying. She's also been forgetting to turn off the stove, and I found a burned pot yesterday. I want to look into memory care facilities, but my sister says Mom would be heartbroken if we put her in a home and that we should honor her wishes to stay at home. Mom gets very agitated when I bring it up and says I'm trying to get rid of her. I feel guilty even thinking about it. Maybe I should just try harder to keep her safe at home myself?

I can really feel how torn you are between your mother's safety and your love for her. It's so hard when the person you're trying to protect is resisting the help they need. I understand your sister's concern, but what stands out to me are the serious safety risks: wandering at night and leaving the stove on. These suggest her needs may be exceeding what can safely be managed at home. Memory care isn't about getting rid of her, it's about providing a secure environment where she can get the supervision and care she needs while staying safe. The guilt you feel is normal, but your mother's safety is paramount. I'd recommend consulting with a geriatric care manager or her doctor to get an objective assessment of her needs. They can help you evaluate memory care options that prioritize her well-being and dignity. You're not failing her by considering this; you're being a responsible caregiver.

I'm a 30-year-old woman who grew up in a very conservative religious community. I left the community three years ago, but my 17-year-old sister is still there. She's about to be married to a 34-year-old man from our former church. She barely knows him — they've only met a few times with chaperones. She's told me she doesn't want to marry him but feels she has no choice because our parents have already accepted the dowry and it would bring shame on the family if she backs out. She's been crying every time we talk. I'm the only one she's told how she really feels. If I report this to child protective services or try to get her out, I could be cut off from my family entirely and she might never speak to me again. Should I respect her wishes and stay out of it?

I'm deeply concerned for your sister's safety and well-being. She is a minor, and being forced into a marriage she doesn't want is a serious form of abuse and coercion. While I understand your fear of losing contact with her and your family, her safety must come first. I strongly recommend contacting child protective services or a trusted organization like the National Domestic Violence Hotline or a legal aid group that specializes in forced marriage. They can offer guidance on how to intervene in a way that minimizes risk to her and your relationship. You are not betraying her trust by protecting her; you are showing her that her feelings and autonomy matter. Please take action now to ensure she has the chance to make her own choices about her future.

My 82-year-old grandmother with Alzheimer's lives with my uncle. Last week when I visited, she had a large bruise on her arm and seemed scared of my uncle. When I asked her about it, she whispered 'he gets so angry when I forget things.' My uncle says she's clumsy and falls a lot. He's her primary caregiver and says he's under a lot of stress. I'm the only other family member who visits regularly. Should I call Adult Protective Services, or would that just make things worse?

I'm really glad you're taking this seriously. Your grandmother's fear and her whispered statement are very concerning, especially combined with the bruise. While caregiver stress is real, it never justifies causing fear or injury. The fact that she's scared of your uncle is a red flag, and her Alzheimer's doesn't mean her perception of danger is invalid—in fact, individuals with dementia can be more vulnerable to abuse. I strongly recommend you call Adult Protective Services immediately. They can conduct a confidential investigation to ensure her safety. You can also document the bruise and any other observations. If you're worried about your uncle's reaction, APS can often keep your identity anonymous. Additionally, consider reaching out to your grandmother's doctor or a local elder abuse hotline for guidance. Your priority must be her safety. Please don't hesitate—this is exactly the kind of situation APS is meant to address.

My 42-year-old brother has a traumatic brain injury from a car accident. He lives in a group home. His caregiver, a 55-year-old woman, has been pressuring him to sign over his disability checks to her. She says she'll manage his money better. He's confused and scared but he likes her and doesn't want to cause trouble. I'm worried this is financial exploitation. Should I report this to adult protective services?

I can hear how concerned you are for your brother. This is a really difficult situation. Yes, you should absolutely report this to adult protective services. What you've described sounds like clear financial exploitation, and your brother is in a vulnerable position due to his brain injury. Reporting is the right way to protect him, and APS can investigate discreetly without immediately disrupting his life. They can also connect him with a trusted financial advocate. It's natural to worry about your relationship, but keeping him safe is the priority. You can explain to him that you're doing this out of love and to ensure he's treated fairly.

My 28-year-old brother has schizophrenia and lives in a supported living group home. I visited him yesterday and noticed he had a large bruise on his face. When I asked him about it, he said one of the staff members hit him when he wouldn't take his medication. He seemed very scared and asked me not to say anything because he's afraid he'll get kicked out. The staff members are usually nice, and my brother can sometimes be paranoid. I'm not sure if this really happened or if he's confused. Should I report this to the state agency that oversees the home, or should I talk to the home's manager first? I don't want to cause trouble if it's just his paranoia.

This is a very serious situation that requires immediate and appropriate action to ensure your brother's safety. Even if your brother's report might be influenced by his paranoia, the possibility of abuse cannot be ignored. It is crucial to report this to the state agency that oversees the home, as they are trained to investigate such allegations thoroughly and impartially. Additionally, you should not discuss this with the home's manager first, as that could jeopardize the investigation and potentially put your brother at risk. The state agency will also be able to ensure your brother's safety and stability throughout the process. Remember, reporting suspected abuse is not causing trouble—it is protecting a vulnerable person from potential harm.

My 16-year-old daughter has been eating very little for the past two months. She's lost about 15 pounds and is now underweight. She obsessively counts calories and exercises for two hours every day. She gets angry if I try to get her to eat more. Her pediatrician recommended an eating disorder specialist, but my daughter refuses to go. She says she's fine and I'm being controlling. I'm worried she'll get worse. Should I force her to see the specialist anyway, or should I respect her autonomy and let her come to terms with it on her own?

I hear how worried you are, and that's completely understandable. Eating disorders are serious medical conditions that require professional treatment. The pediatrician's recommendation to see a specialist is crucial here. While respecting autonomy is important, your daughter's health is in danger—she's underweight and showing clear signs of an eating disorder. Forcing her into treatment isn't about control; it's about saving her life. I strongly recommend you follow the pediatrician's advice and insist on the specialist, possibly involving child protective services if needed to ensure she gets the care she requires. Your relationship can be repaired later, but her health cannot wait. Please prioritize her safety over her immediate feelings.

I'm a gymnastics coach. One of the other coaches, a man in his 40s, has been spending a lot of one-on-one time with a 13-year-old girl on the team. He gives her extra private 'stretching sessions' after practice with the door closed. Yesterday she seemed upset and told me he makes her feel uncomfortable and touches her in ways that don't seem like normal stretching. She begged me not to tell anyone because she's afraid she'll get kicked off the team and lose her dream of competing. I'm not sure what I actually saw or heard - I don't have proof. If I report this to the gym owner or the police and it turns out to be nothing, I could destroy his career and reputation, and the girl might be traumatized by the investigation. Should I just keep an eye on the situation and wait for more concrete evidence before saying anything?

I hear how difficult this is, and I can understand your concern about making a mistake. But I want to be very clear: what you've described is a potential case of child sexual abuse. The girl has directly told you she feels uncomfortable and that the touching doesn't seem like normal stretching. That is a disclosure, and it is your responsibility to report it. You don't need proof—that's for investigators to determine. By reporting, you are protecting the child and potentially preventing further harm. If you're worried about the impact on the coach, remember that the child's safety comes first. You can report to the gym owner and also to your local child protective services or law enforcement. They will handle the investigation sensitively. The girl's fear of being kicked off the team is understandable, but she needs to know that you are on her side and that her wellbeing matters more than any dream. Please do not wait for more evidence. Report now.

My 13-year-old son has been talking about suicide. He told me that sometimes he thinks about 'not being here anymore' and that he feels like a burden to everyone. He made me promise not to tell anyone, especially not his dad or a therapist. He said if I tell anyone, he'll never trust me again and he'll just stop talking to me about how he feels. I'm terrified that if I break his trust, he'll shut me out completely and I won't be able to help him at all. Should I keep his confidence and just try to be there for him, or should I tell someone even if it means he might not talk to me anymore?

I can hear how scared you are, and this is one of the hardest positions a parent can be in. The fact that he's talking to you about it is actually a really good sign — it means he trusts you, and that trust is a lifeline. However, when a child expresses suicidal thoughts, safety has to come first. Keeping his promise could put him at risk. I strongly recommend that you tell someone who can help, like his dad, a therapist, or a crisis professional. You can explain to your son that you love him too much to keep a secret that could hurt him, and that your goal is to get him support, not to betray him. You might say, 'I hear that you don't want me to tell anyone, but my job as your parent is to keep you safe, and I need to get help for you.' It's possible he'll be angry or feel betrayed, but that's a temporary feeling. Your long-term relationship will be stronger if he's alive and healthy. Please call a crisis line or take him to the emergency room if you're worried about immediate danger. Your love and courage to act can save his life.

My 16-year-old son was diagnosed with Hodgkin's lymphoma. The doctors say it's very treatable with chemotherapy and radiation, with a 90% cure rate. But my son is terrified of the side effects - losing his hair, being sick, missing school. He's been reading online about alternative treatments like special diets, supplements, and herbal remedies. He wants to try those first and only do chemo if they don't work. His oncologist says delaying treatment could be dangerous. My son is usually very mature and responsible. He's begging me to respect his decision and let him try alternatives for a few months. I don't want to damage our relationship by forcing him into treatment he doesn't want. Should I let him try the alternative approach first and see if it helps?

I can hear how torn you are between your son's wishes and what the doctors recommend. It's a very difficult position for any parent. However, as his parent, your primary responsibility is to protect his health and safety. With a highly treatable cancer like Hodgkin's lymphoma where delay can reduce the cure rate, it would be dangerous to postpone proven treatment. While respecting his autonomy is important, a 16-year-old may not fully grasp the risks of delaying chemotherapy. I strongly recommend you follow the oncologist's advice to start treatment immediately. You can address his fears by connecting him with a child life specialist or counselor who can help him cope with side effects, and explore complementary approaches like a healthy diet alongside, not instead of, standard medical care. Your relationship with your son may face some strain, but his life and health must come first. In the long run, he will likely understand that you made the difficult but right choice.

My 82-year-old mother has early-stage dementia and lives with my younger brother, who is her primary caregiver. I live three hours away and visit once a month. Over the past few months, I've noticed some concerning changes. She seems thinner, and my brother says she's just 'eating less because of old age.' Her checking account, which I'm also on, shows regular withdrawals of $200-300 that my brother says are for 'supplies and medications,' but the amounts don't match any receipts I've seen. Last visit, Mom seemed confused about money and mentioned my brother 'helping her with her bills.' When I asked my brother directly, he got defensive and said I'm being paranoid and that I don't know how much work it is to care for her. My mom is happy living with him and says she trusts him completely. I don't want to accuse my brother of something awful and tear our family apart if I'm wrong. Should I contact Adult Protective Services, or should I talk to my brother again and try to get more information first?

This is a very concerning situation, and I appreciate you reaching out. Your mother's safety and well-being must come first, even if it risks family tension. The combination of unexplained weight loss, unaccounted financial withdrawals, and defensive behavior from your brother are red flags that warrant formal investigation. I strongly recommend contacting Adult Protective Services now. They are trained to handle these situations sensitively and can assess whether your mother is at risk of financial exploitation or neglect. Your brother may be overwhelmed, but that doesn't excuse potential misuse of funds or inadequate care. By involving APS, you are not necessarily accusing your brother; you are ensuring your mother gets the protection she needs. If your brother is innocent, an investigation will clarify things, and you can then work together to get her proper care. Please prioritize reporting over another potentially confrontational conversation. You can call the National Adult Protective Services hotline at 1-833-910-0516 for guidance.

I'm a high school counselor. One of my 15-year-old students told me in confidence that she's been meeting a 34-year-old man she met online. He tells her she's 'wise beyond her years' and that their connection is special. They text constantly, and he's sent her gifts including a necklace. She's asked me not to tell her parents because they'd 'overreact' and she'd lose his trust. She says nothing sexual has happened but he's told her he loves her and they've talked about running away together after she turns 16, since 'the age of consent in our state is 16.' I know that as a counselor I'm a mandated reporter, but if I report this and nothing has actually happened yet, I could destroy this girl's trust in me and in the system. She might just stop talking to any adult altogether. Should I report this to CPS now, or should I keep meeting with her to build trust and try to convince her to end the relationship herself?

I understand how torn you feel, but as a mandated reporter, you have a legal and ethical obligation to report this situation to Child Protective Services immediately. The fact that the man is 34, she is 15, and he has discussed running away together and professed love is a clear red flag for grooming and potential sexual abuse. Your duty to protect her from harm outweighs the risk of losing her trust. Reporting now does not mean you end your relationship with her—you can explain that you are required to do this to keep her safe, and you will continue to support her. Inaction could leave her vulnerable to further manipulation and harm. Please report it today.

I'm a middle school counselor. A 13-year-old student told me that her stepfather has been coming into her room at night and touching her inappropriately. She made me promise not to tell anyone because she's scared of what will happen if her mom finds out. I'm a mandated reporter - I know I have to report this. But I'm worried about traumatizing the girl further if CPS gets involved, and about destroying the family. Should I report it immediately, or should I try to talk to the mother first to get more context?

I can hear how difficult this situation is for you. You're trying to balance your legal obligations with your desire to protect the student from additional trauma. It's important to remember that your role as a mandated reporter means you have a legal duty to report suspected child abuse immediately. While you care about the student's trust, her safety is the top priority. Talking to the mother first could give the stepfather time to cover up the abuse or pressure the child to recant. Reporting to CPS now ensures that trained professionals can investigate while protecting the child. You can explain to the student that you must keep her safe, even if it feels like a betrayal. The system is designed to minimize further trauma, and you can support her throughout the process. Please report right away.

I'm a home health aide supervisor. One of my aides, a woman in her 50s, has been assigned to an 88-year-old client with moderate dementia who lives alone. The client's daughter, who lives out of state, called me concerned because her mother's credit card bills show hundreds of dollars in online shopping charges that don't make sense - subscriptions to streaming services, food delivery, and clothing that her mother has never used before. The daughter also noticed that $2,000 has been transferred from her mother's savings account to what appears to be a personal payment app. The aide has been with the client for six months and the client adores her, saying she's 'like a daughter.' When I asked the aide about it casually, she said the client must have given her passwords to 'help with online shopping' because the client gets confused. I don't have any hard proof that the aide is doing anything wrong. If I report this to Adult Protective Services or the police, I could ruin this aide's career and reputation over a misunderstanding. The client might also get very upset and refuse care from anyone else. Should I just switch the aide to a different client and see if the suspicious charges stop, or should I report this to authorities now?

I understand your concern about the potential impact on the aide's career and the client's reactions, but this situation raises serious red flags for financial exploitation of a vulnerable adult. The pattern of unauthorized charges, transfers to a payment app, and the aide's access to passwords all point to a need for immediate investigation. Your primary duty is to protect the client, not to avoid potential embarrassment or conflict. I strongly recommend reporting this to Adult Protective Services and local law enforcement today. They are trained to handle such allegations discreetly and can investigate without prematurely accusing the aide. If the aide is innocent, the investigation will clear her name. If she is guilty, you will have prevented further financial harm to the client. Additionally, you should notify the client's daughter and involve the client's bank to freeze any further unauthorized transactions. Switching the aide to another client would only enable the exploitation to potentially shift to another victim and would not address the current situation. Please report this now.

My 12-year-old nephew has been telling me that his dad (my brother) locks him in his room for hours at a time as punishment. Sometimes from right after school until bedtime, with no dinner. His dad also calls him horrible names - 'stupid', 'worthless', 'a mistake' - nearly every day. The boy is depressed, has started hurting himself by cutting his arms, and told me he thinks about killing himself. When I confronted my brother, he said I don't know how to raise a kid and that this is just normal discipline to teach respect. He said his kid is just dramatic and looking for attention. My nephew begged me not to tell anyone because he's scared his dad will get even worse if he finds out I said something. I'm not a mandated reporter in my state. Should I call CPS anyway, or should I just keep being a supportive aunt and try to get my nephew help on my own without involving authorities?

This is an extremely serious situation that requires immediate action to protect your nephew. Your nephew is showing clear signs of abuse including physical confinement, verbal abuse, self-harm, and suicidal ideation. These factors outweigh concerns about potential retaliation or your brother's reaction. I strongly recommend calling Child Protective Services right away. If you are hesitant to call CPS directly, you can also call the National Child Abuse Hotline at 1-800-422-4453. They can provide confidential guidance on how to report on behalf of a child in danger. Additionally, if your nephew is in immediate risk of suicide, call 988 or take him to the nearest emergency room. Your role as a supportive aunt is important, but in this case, your nephew's safety must come first. Reporting is a legal and ethical obligation to prevent further harm.

I'm the mother of a 13-year-old girl. She came to me crying because some classmates created a fake Instagram account using her photos and name, and posted embarrassing and sexual comments pretending to be her. She's distraught and doesn't want to go to school. I want to call the school principal and file a report, and possibly involve the police since the content is sexual. But my daughter is begging me not to because she's terrified of the bullies finding out she told, and says it will make things worse. She's also scared that the school will confiscate her phone and she'll be even more isolated. My husband thinks we should handle it ourselves by contacting the parents of the kids we suspect. I don't want to traumatize my daughter further by forcing a big investigation that might not lead anywhere. Should I just help her block the accounts and change her privacy settings, and monitor things at home, or should I escalate to the school and police?

I can hear how upsetting this is for both you and your daughter. I strongly recommend that you escalate this to the school and the police. Creating a fake account with sexual content involving a minor is a serious offense, possibly even illegal, and addressing it through official channels is important for protecting your daughter and preventing harm to others. You can explain to your daughter that reporting is about stopping the bullying and holding the perpetrators accountable, and that you'll support her through the process. Work with the school and police to ensure her privacy is respected and that she feels safe. While her fears are understandable, allowing this to go unaddressed could lead to further escalation. Contacting the parents directly might not be effective and could even worsen the situation. Blocking the account and adjusting settings are good temporary measures, but they don't resolve the underlying issue. Please reach out to the school principal and local authorities as soon as possible.

My 15-year-old daughter has been diagnosed with anorexia nervosa. She's lost a dangerous amount of weight and her heart rate is dangerously low. The doctor wants to hospitalize her for medical stabilization and refeeding. But my daughter is terrified of the hospital - she says they'll force-feed her and make her gain weight too fast, and that she'll lose control of her body. She's begging me not to make her go. She's promised to eat more at home and see a therapist. I'm worried that if I force her into the hospital, she'll never trust me again and will just get better at hiding her eating disorder. She's a smart, capable girl and I want to respect her autonomy. Should I try to manage this at home with outpatient therapy instead, at least for now, and only consider hospitalization if she gets worse?

I can hear how torn you are between what the doctors recommend and what your daughter wants. It's such a difficult position to be in as a parent. However, when a patient has dangerously low weight and a critically low heart rate, immediate medical stabilization is life-saving. Hospitalization is not about punishment or control; it's about stopping physical decline and preventing organ failure. Forcing her into the hospital now, though heartbreaking, is an act of love and responsibility. Once she is medically stable, she can continue recovery with outpatient therapy, including family-based treatment, and rebuilding trust. Her life and long-term health must come first.
